content: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. {{v:2}} The same was in the beginning with God. {{v:3}} All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. {{v:4}} In him was life, and the life was the light of men. {{v:5}} The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

facets.text: The Prologue opens by declaring the eternal preexistence of the Word: before creation, in the timeless "beginning," the Word already "was." This Word is both distinct from God ("with God") and fully divine ("was God"), safeguarding at once the unity of the divine nature and the real distinction of persons. Against every later denial, the text affirms that the Son is not a creature but truly God, coeternal with the Father.
facets.question: Was the Word truly God from all eternity, or a created being?

facets.text: By echoing Genesis 1:1 ("In the beginning"), John presents the incarnate Word as the very agent of creation: "All things were made through him." Nothing that exists came to be apart from him, so the whole created order bears the imprint of the divine Word. The One who redeems is the same One through whom the universe was first spoken into being.
facets.question: What role does the Word play in the creation of all things?

facets.text: The passage names the Word as the source of life itself—"In him was life"—and identifies that life as "the light of men." Creation and salvation are joined: the life that sustains all things is also the illuminating truth that draws humanity toward God. This life is not merely biological but the divine life that enlightens minds and hearts.
facets.question: How is Christ both the source of life and the light of humanity?

facets.text: The image of light shining in darkness that the darkness could not overcome portrays the drama of redemption. Darkness signifies sin, ignorance, and the powers opposed to God, yet it has no power to extinguish the divine light. The verse quietly anticipates the victory of the cross and resurrection, assuring that evil can resist but never conquer the light of the Word.
facets.question: Can the darkness of sin and evil ever overcome the light of Christ?

facets.text: Calling the Son "the Word" (Logos) teaches that God expresses and reveals himself perfectly in the person of the Son. As a word makes thought known, the eternal Word makes the invisible God known and is the fullness of divine self-communication. This grounds the whole Gospel: to encounter Jesus is to encounter God's own utterance and truth.
facets.question: Why does John call the Son the Word (Logos) of God?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The Johannine Prologue proclaims the eternal preexistence, full divinity, and creative agency of the Word, who is the source of life and light and whose light the darkness cannot overcome. Its scope is foundational Christology, Trinitarian distinction, and the creation-redemption unity.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The Word eternally "was," is "with God" and "was God," affirming the Son's coeternal divinity and real distinction from the Father against Arian and modalist errors.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: Echoing Genesis 1:1, all things were made through the Word, so the Redeemer is the very agent of creation and nothing exists apart from him.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The Word is the source of life that is also "the light of men," uniting creation and salvation in the divine life that enlightens humanity.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The light shining in darkness that darkness cannot overcome dramatizes redemption's victory over sin, ignorance, and evil, anticipating the cross and resurrection.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Naming the Son "Logos" teaches that God reveals and communicates himself perfectly in the Son, so encountering Jesus is encountering God's own utterance.

content: Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him. {{v:2}} He opened his mouth and taught them, saying, {{v:3}} “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. {{v:4}} Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. {{v:5}} Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth. {{v:6}} Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. {{v:7}} Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. {{v:8}} Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. {{v:9}} Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. {{v:10}} Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. {{v:11}} “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake. {{v:12}} Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

facets.text: Jesus ascends the mountain, sits as the authoritative teacher, and opens the Sermon on the Mount, presenting himself as the new Moses who gives a new and interior law. Whereas Moses received the Law at Sinai, Christ himself is the lawgiver who teaches from the mountain with his own authority. The Beatitudes thus open the definitive charter of the Kingdom of Heaven.
facets.question: Why does Jesus teach the Beatitudes from a mountain?

facets.text: The Beatitudes reveal that true blessedness is found not in earthly power, wealth, or comfort, but in dispositions the world considers weakness: poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, hunger for righteousness. They overturn worldly standards of happiness by locating beatitude in God and his Kingdom rather than in visible goods. This teaching draws the human heart toward its ultimate end, the vision and possession of God.
facets.question: Where does true happiness and blessedness actually come from?

facets.text: Poverty of spirit, placed first, is the foundational disposition of the Kingdom: a humble recognition of one's total dependence on God and detachment from riches and self-sufficiency. To such humble souls the Kingdom of Heaven already belongs in the present tense, marking them as the true heirs. This spiritual poverty makes room in the heart for grace and for God himself.
facets.question: What does it mean to be poor in spirit?

facets.text: Each beatitude joins a present disposition to a promised divine reward—comfort, inheritance of the earth, satisfaction, mercy, the vision of God, divine sonship—showing that grace works both now and in fulfilled glory. The rewards are eschatological gifts of God's own life, culminating in seeing God face to face, the beatific vision. The structure teaches that the Christian life is ordered toward a reward that God alone gives.
facets.question: What rewards do the Beatitudes promise and when are they fulfilled?

facets.text: The promise that the pure in heart shall see God identifies the ultimate goal of human existence as the beatific vision, granted to those whose hearts are cleansed of sin and divided love. Purity of heart is not merely moral cleanliness but an undivided orientation of the whole person toward God. The vision of God is both the reward and the fulfillment of that singleness of heart.
facets.question: What does it mean that the pure in heart will see God?

facets.text: The peacemakers are called children of God because they participate in the reconciling work of God himself, who reconciles the world to himself in Christ. To make peace is to share in the divine sonship, imaging the Father who is the source of true peace. This beatitude reveals that Christian identity is bound to the ministry of reconciliation.
facets.question: Why are peacemakers called children of God?

facets.text: The final beatitudes declare blessed those persecuted for righteousness and reproached falsely for Christ's sake, uniting the disciples' suffering with a great heavenly reward. By linking their persecution to that of the prophets before them, Jesus places his followers within the prophetic tradition and foreshadows the cross. Suffering endured for his sake becomes a cause not of despair but of exceeding joy.
facets.question: Why should Christians rejoice when they are persecuted for their faith?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The opening of the Sermon on the Mount presents the Beatitudes as the charter of the Kingdom, revealing true blessedness in God-centered dispositions and their eschatological rewards, culminating in the vision of God and the joy of suffering for Christ.

[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Jesus teaching from the mountain acts as the new Moses and divine lawgiver giving a new interior law from his own authority.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: True blessedness lies not in wealth or power but in God and his Kingdom, overturning worldly notions of happiness.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Poverty of spirit, the foundational Kingdom disposition, is humble dependence on God to whom the Kingdom already belongs.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Each beatitude pairs a present disposition with a God-given reward, both now and in fulfilled glory, ordered toward the beatific vision.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The pure in heart will see God, making the beatific vision the goal of an undivided heart cleansed of sin.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Peacemakers are called children of God by sharing in his reconciling work and divine sonship.
[MORAL | explicit]: Those persecuted and slandered for Christ's sake are blessed, joined to the prophets and called to rejoice for their heavenly reward.
